title: Charcoal Briquettes 8kg

drivers.name: 20% off promotion
drivers.evidence: Past promotions show median x0.83 vs baseline; noise-adjusted x1.0. One 25% off during holiday hit x4.58. This 20% off is deeper than 10% and 15% off events, and timing is post-Labor Day, when demand is low. Historical uplifts are inconsistent, so we apply moderate uplift.

drivers.name: Store closed Monday
drivers.evidence: Store closure on Monday reduces 1/7 of the week's sales potential. No past data on closures, but standard practice is to reduce sales by ~14% for single-day closures.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 28.3. A 20% price discount is a strong driver, but past promotions show mixed results: median uplift x0.83, noise-adjusted x1.0. However, one 30% off promo saw x2.53, and a 25% off during Independence Day hit x4.58—suggesting potential for high uplift in high-demand weeks. This week is 4 weeks post-Labor Day, a seasonal lull (recent sales: 13–34 units), but the promotion may counteract decline. Store closure on Monday reduces 1/7 of the week, so we reduce demand by ~14%. The classical model's x1.0 is too low; we adjust up for the deep discount and event timing, but shrink toward 1.0 due to sparse, noisy past data. No prior 20% off promo, so uncertainty is high.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 28.3 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 74.0 | 10%-90%: 5.9 - 51.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-73% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
